mainTopic: Does someone who deserves a court punishment (death or מלקות), but is not actually punished, still have to pay money for the damage he caused? The dispute between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
overview: This amud continues the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about someone whose act carries a court punishment and also causes money damage, when the punishment is not actually given. First the גמרא finishes a back-and-forth over the פסוק "ולא יהיה אסון". It gives two versions of who challenged whom, and each side reads the word אסון in its own favor. Then רבא challenges the whole setup: the ברייתא of דבי חזקיה shows that anyone whose act carries the death penalty never pays, even if the act was unintentional. So רבין reports a new version: everyone agrees about חייבי מיתות, and the argument is only about חייבי מלקות. רבי יוחנן says they pay, because only מיתה was compared to money. ריש לקיש says they are exempt, because the Torah included מלקות too. The גמרא asks for ריש לקיש's source. אביי learns it from the word 'רשע'. רבא learns it from 'הכאה', using the injury פסוק for a blow worth less than a פרוטה, which gets lashes.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's challenge: the verse means real death
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש finishes his challenge: in the פסוק "ולא יהיה אסון", the word אסון must mean the woman actually died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Doesn't it mean actual harm, that the woman really died?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes ריש לקיש's challenge to רבי יוחנן. He reads the פסוק about the pregnant woman as saying that if she actually dies, the attacker does not pay for the baby.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אסון means the woman really died, the Torah is saying: when a death-penalty sin happened, there is no payment, even if the attacker is never executed. That supports ריש לקיש, who says such a person is exempt from paying, and goes against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Doesn't it mean...? (a way of pushing a reading as the obvious one)
Harm, a tragedy; here, the woman's death

phrases.english: Is it not referring to actual harm!
phrases.notes: This goes back to the פסוק about men fighting who hit a pregnant woman (שמות 21:22). Actual harm means she really died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes ריש לקיש's objection from the פסוק, which began just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's view that someone who deserves death but is not executed still pays.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק makes payment depend on whether the woman actually died, not on whether the attacker was executed. So once a death-penalty sin happened, there is no payment at all.

steps.title: Answer: the verse means a death sentence
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's side answers that אסון means a court sentence of death, not just the death itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means a sentence of harm, meaning a death sentence from the court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by reading the word אסון differently: it means the court actually sentences the attacker to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this reading, the פסוק says: as long as the attacker is not actually sentenced and executed, he pays for the baby. That fits רבי יוחנן perfectly, so ריש לקיש's challenge falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: A sentence of harm, meaning a court ruling of death

phrases.english: No, it means a sentence of harm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by re-reading the key word.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אסון means the woman really died, so there is never payment.
steps.terutzMaskana: אסון means an actual death sentence. Without one, the attacker pays.

steps.title: Other version: רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש from the same verse
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, it was רבי יוחנן who challenged ריש לקיש from the same פסוק, reading אסון as a death sentence.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say it went the other way: רבי יוחנן challenged ריש לקיש from "And there is no harm, he shall surely be punished." Doesn't it mean a sentence of harm?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same argument, with the roles flipped. Now רבי יוחנן uses the פסוק against ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אסון means a death sentence, the פסוק teaches that without an actual sentence the attacker pays. That goes against ריש לקיש, who says he is exempt even when he is not executed.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection against him
He shall surely be punished (with money)

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions use the exact same פסוק and the same two readings. The only change is who is attacking and who is defending.

phrases.english: Some say:
Rabbi Yoḥanan raised an objection to Reish Lakish:
"And there is no harm, he shall surely be punished";
is it not referring to a sentence of harm?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Retells steps 1-2 with the challenger and the defender switched.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that someone who deserves death is exempt from paying even if he is not executed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If payment depends on whether there was a death sentence, then without a sentence he pays, which goes against ריש לקיש.

steps.title: Answer: the verse means real death
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that אסון means the woman actually died.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש defends himself by reading אסון as the real death of the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the woman really died, a death-penalty sin happened, so there is no payment even without an execution. That fits ריש לקיש. Neither version of the פסוק debate settles the argument.
steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק "ולא יהיה אסון" can be read two ways: real death, which helps ריש לקיש, or a death sentence, which helps רבי יוחנן. So it proves nothing either way.

phrases.english: No, it means actual harm.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: אסון means a death sentence, so without one he pays.
steps.terutzMaskana: אסון means real death, so there is no payment even without an execution.

steps.title: רבא: how could anyone say they must pay?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks how anyone could hold that people who deserve death for an unintentional sin still have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Is there really anyone who says that people who did a death-penalty sin unwittingly must pay?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the whole way the argument was set up. He finds רבי יוחנן's position, as described so far, impossible to hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a real question asking for information. It is a challenge to the premise that רבי יוחנן makes חייבי מיתות pay. The next step gives the source behind רבא's objection.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there anyone who says...? (a rhetorical challenge)
People who deserve the death penalty
Unintentional, without the conditions for actual punishment

steps.confusionAlert: Here שוגגין refers to cases where the court cannot actually carry out the punishment. The whole question is whether money is owed when no punishment is given.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Is there anyone who says
that those liable to death who acted unwittingly are obligated to pay?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps back from the debate over the פסוק and challenges the basic description of רבי יוחנן's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוחנן obligates חייבי מיתות שוגגין to pay.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A known ברייתא (step 6) clearly exempts anyone whose act carries the death penalty from paying, with no exceptions.

steps.title: The teaching of דבי חזקיה: hitting a person vs. hitting an animal
steps.stepSummary: דבי חזקיה compares one who hits an animal, who always pays, with one who kills a person, who never pays, with no exceptions for intent or type of motion.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the school of חזקיה taught: "one who hits a person" and "one who hits an animal" are set side by side. Just as with hitting an animal you make no distinction between accidental and deliberate, intending and not intending, a downward or an upward blow, and in every case it is to make him pay, never to exempt him, so with hitting a person, make no distinction between accidental and deliberate, intending and not intending, downward or upward, and in every case it is to exempt him from paying, never to make him pay.
steps.whatsHappening: This is רבא's proof. The Torah sets the two cases side by side: hitting an animal always means paying, and killing a person always means no payment, even when the killing was unintentional.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since an unintentional killer is never executed by the court, this ברייתא shows that a person whose act carries the death penalty is exempt from money even when he is not actually punished. So no one could say חייבי מיתות שוגגין must pay, and רבי יוחנן's view must be about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching from the study hall of חזקיה
While moving downward / while moving upward
To exempt him from paying money

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the anchor for the rule that a death-penalty act cancels any money payment for the same act, even if no execution takes place. It forces the whole argument to be reframed.

phrases.english: But didn't the school of Ḥizkiyya teach:
"One who smites a person" and "one who smites an animal":
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:21. The two cases appear in the same פסוק, so they are compared.

phrases.english: just as with one who smites an animal
you did not distinguish in it
between unwitting and intentional,
between one who intended and one who did not intend,
between a downward motion and an upward motion,
not to exempt him from money, but rather to obligate him to pay money;

phrases.aramaic: אַף מַכֵּה אָדָם לֹא תַּחְלוֹק בּוֹ
phrases.english: so too with one who smites a person, do not distinguish in it
between unwitting and intentional,
between one who intended and one who did not intend,
between a downward motion and an upward motion:
not to obligate him to pay money, but rather to exempt him from money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind רבא's challenge in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That חייבי מיתות שוגגין are exempt from paying money.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of דבי חזקיה, comparing מכה אדם to מכה בהמה from ויקרא 24:21.

steps.title: רבין's version: the argument is only about lashes
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports that everyone agrees חייבי מיתות שוגגין are exempt. The argument is about someone who deserves מלקות and also owes money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said: About those who deserve death and acted unwittingly, everyone agrees they are exempt. Where they disagree is about those who deserve lashes and acted unwittingly, when there is also another matter, a money payment.
steps.whatsHappening: Because of רבא's challenge, the גמרא drops the earlier version and brings רבין's report of what the argument really is. This sets up the two opinions in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא of דבי חזקיה settles the death-penalty case, so no one argues about it. The open question moves to sins that carry מלקות: if the מלקות are not given, does the person pay for the damage?

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
Another matter, a money obligation from the same act

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came, he said:
those liable to death who acted unwittingly:
everyone agrees that they are exempt.
When they disagree,
it is about those liable to lashes who acted unwittingly, together with another matter.
phrases.notes: Another matter means a money payment that comes from the same act.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge by moving the argument from מיתה to מלקות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining what the argument is about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש argue about חייבי מיתות שוגגין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone exempts חייבי מיתות. They argue only about חייבי מלקות who also owe money.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: lashes were not compared, so he pays
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the person who deserves מלקות must pay, because only מיתה was compared by the Torah to the money case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said he must pay: those who deserve death were compared (to money cases), but those who deserve lashes were not compared.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives his ruling and his reason: the היקש of דבי חזקיה covers only death-penalty cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's comparison is limited to מכה אדם, which is a death-penalty case. מלקות were not part of it, so the normal rule applies: unless he is actually given מלקות, he pays for the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Were compared by a היקש (set side by side in the פסוק)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: he is obligated to pay;
those liable to death were juxtaposed,
phrases.notes: This means the comparison of מכה אדם with מכה בהמה from the previous teaching.

phrases.english: those liable to lashes were not juxtaposed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first side of the argument defined by רבין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who deserves מלקות but is not given them pays for the damage, because the exemption comes only from the היקש, which covers death-penalty cases.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: the Torah included lashes, so he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says the person is exempt, because the Torah clearly treats חייבי מלקות like חייבי מיתות.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said he is exempt: the Torah explicitly included those who deserve lashes like those who deserve death.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives the opposite ruling: the exemption from paying applies to מלקות cases too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש agrees the היקש alone is about death, but he holds that the Torah clearly added מלקות to the same rule. So a person whose act carries מלקות is exempt from paying for that act, even if no מלקות are given.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah included (added to the rule)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבין, everyone exempts חייבי מיתות שוגגין from money because of the ברייתא of דבי חזקיה. The argument is about מלקות: רבי יוחנן says he pays because מלקות were not compared, and ריש לקיש says he is exempt because the Torah clearly included מלקות.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said: he is exempt;
the Torah explicitly included
those liable to lashes like those liable to death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing side to רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who deserves מלקות is exempt from paying for the same act, because the Torah explicitly put מלקות in the same category as מיתה.

steps.title: Where does the Torah include those who get lashes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the Torah teaches that חייבי מלקות are treated like חייבי מיתות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where did the Torah include them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks ריש לקיש for his source. Where does the Torah put people who get מלקות in the same group as people who get מיתה? This question sets up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש said the Torah 'included' חייבי מלקות with חייבי מיתות, so they are also exempt from paying. Now the גמרא wants the actual פסוק or derivation behind that claim.

phrases.english: Where did the Torah include [those who get lashes]?
phrases.notes: This points back to ריש לקיש in step 9, who said the Torah treats lashes like death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind ריש לקיש's statement in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source that puts חייבי מלקות together with חייבי מיתות.

steps.title: אביי: learned from the word 'wicked'
steps.stepSummary: אביי derives it through a גזירה שוה on the word 'רשע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that the word 'רשע' (wicked) appears both by someone who deserves death and by someone who deserves lashes. That shared word links the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Torah calls both the death-deserver and the lashes-deserver 'רשע', they are treated the same way. Just as the death-deserver does not pay money, the lashes-deserver does not pay either.

keyTerms.meaning: Linking two פסוקים through a shared word

phrases.english: Abaye said:
It is learned from 'wicked' and 'wicked'.
phrases.notes: One is במדבר 35:31 ('wicked, deserving to die'); the other is דברים 25:2 ('if the wicked deserves lashes').

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on the word 'רשע' links מלקות to מיתה.

steps.title: רבא: learned from the word 'hits'
steps.stepSummary: רבא offers a different source: a link built on the word 'מכה' (one who hits).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is learned from 'hits' and 'hits'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different source. He builds the link on the word 'מכה' (one who hits) instead of 'רשע'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא agrees there is a link, but he finds it in the hitting פסוקים of ויקרא 24. The next steps ask exactly which פסוקים he means.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is learned from 'hits' and 'hits'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 10, different from אביי's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A link built on the word 'מכה'.

steps.title: רב פפא asks which 'hits' רבא means
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks which 'מכה' רבא means. He rejects the obvious one, because that פסוק is about killing, not lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to רבא: Which 'hits'? If you say 'One who hits an animal shall pay for it, and one who hits a person shall be put to death', that is written about killing!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks רבא to point to the exact פסוק. He shows that the first one that comes to mind cannot work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ויקרא 24:21 says hitting an animal means paying, and hitting a person means death. That only teaches about the death-deserver, which we already know is exempt from paying. We still need a 'מכה' that is about a lashes case.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Rava:
Which 'hits' [do you mean]?
If you say: 'And one who hits an animal shall pay for it,'
'and one who hits a person shall be put to death' —
that is written about killing!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְרָבָא הֵי מַכֵּה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which 'מכה' פסוק is about lashes and not about death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That פסוק is about a death case, so it cannot teach anything new about מלקות.

steps.title: The 'hits' רבא means: the injury פסוק next to the animal פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבא's 'מכה' is ויקרא 24:18 about hitting an animal, together with the פסוק right next to it about injuring a person (24:19).
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this 'hits': 'One who hits an animal shall pay for it, a life for a life', and right next to it: 'And a man who puts a blemish in his fellow, as he did so shall be done to him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the right פסוקים. It is the animal-hitting פסוק together with the פסוק right after it, about a person who injures his fellow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hurting a person (24:19) is a case of hitting that can lead to lashes, not death. Through the shared idea of 'hitting', this case is linked to 24:21, where hitting a person brings punishment instead of payment. So the lashes case is also exempt from paying.

keyTerms.meaning: And right next to it is written

phrases.english: Rather, [he means] this 'hits':
'One who hits [and kills] an animal shall pay for it,'
'a life for a life,'
and right next to it [is written]:
'And a man who puts a blemish in his fellow,'
'as he did, so shall be done to him.'
phrases.notes: Some versions include these bracketed words, which just finish the פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's question by naming the correct פסוקים.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא meant ויקרא 24:21, which only deals with death.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא meant 24:18 together with 24:19, a hitting case that is not about death.

steps.title: But that פסוק doesn't say 'hits'
steps.stepSummary: Problem: the injury פסוק says 'puts a blemish', not 'מכה'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's link. A link from a shared word needs the same word in both places, and 24:19 does not use the word 'מכה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the source is 'מכה מכה'. The injury פסוק says 'יתן מום' instead, so the word match seems to be missing.

phrases.english: But this is not [the word] 'hits'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the פסוק picked in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'מכה' does not appear there, so there is no word match.

steps.title: The link is the idea of hitting, not the exact word
steps.stepSummary: The link is based on the shared idea of 'הכאה' (hitting), not on the identical word.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the link is about the idea, not the exact word. Putting a blemish in someone is a kind of hitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים describe an act of hitting, so they match in meaning. That shared idea is enough to connect them.

phrases.english: We are saying 'hitting' and 'hitting'.
phrases.notes: He means the link is the shared idea of a blow, even though the exact word is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording problem raised in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Recasts the link as one of meaning rather than exact wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The link needs the identical word 'מכה'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The shared idea of 'הכאה' is enough.

steps.title: But that פסוק is about injuring, which is paid with money
steps.stepSummary: Problem: 24:19 is about someone who injures his fellow, and such a person pays money. So where are the lashes?
steps.simpleTranslation: But where it is written, it is written about one who injures his fellow, and one who injures his fellow is subject to payment!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second problem. The injury פסוק is about a case where the person pays, so it does not seem to be a lashes case at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To prove that lashes cancel payment, we need a פסוק about someone who gets lashes. But someone who injures his fellow pays damages; he does not get lashes. So the פסוק seems to prove nothing about מלקות.

phrases.english: But when it is written —
it is written about one who injures his fellow,
and one who injures his fellow is subject to payment!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא כִּי כְּתִיב בְּחוֹבֵל בַּחֲבֵירוֹ הוּא דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the פסוק from step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Injuring a person leads to payment, not lashes, so the פסוק cannot teach about חייבי מלקות.

steps.title: Apply it to a blow worth less than a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: Since the פסוק is not needed for a blow worth a פרוטה, it is applied to a blow worth less than a פרוטה, which gets מלקות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is not needed for a blow worth a פרוטה, apply it to a blow that is not worth a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last problem by moving the פסוק to a different case: a blow too small to be worth a פרוטה. In that case there is no money to pay, so the hitter gets lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blow worth a פרוטה or more is paid with money, so the פסוק is not needed there. It is therefore applied to a blow worth less than a פרוטה, which is a lashes case. That gives רבא the lashes case he needs to link to the death case, so חייבי מלקות do not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not needed for this case

steps.whatToRemember: According to ריש לקיש, חייבי מלקות do not pay. אביי learns this from 'רשע רשע'. רבא learns it from 'הכאה הכאה', using the injury פסוק for a blow worth less than a פרוטה, which gets lashes.
steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק about injuring is not saying an injurer who causes real damage gets lashes; he pays. It is applied to lashes only for a blow worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer uses the rule that a blow worth less than a פרוטה, which has no money to pay, is punished with lashes. That makes the injury פסוק a lashes case, which רבא needs for his link.

phrases.english: If it is not needed for a blow
that is worth a perutah —
phrases.notes: That blow is already handled by paying money, so the פסוק isn't needed for it.

phrases.english: apply it to a blow
that is not worth a perutah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לְהַכָּאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 and completes רבא's derivation.
